On this page

Holes given by a conformal map ​

Before this page

Concentration and contribution tensors, for the tensors computed here, and Hill polarization tensors, whose cylindrical case is the elliptic section recovered below.

An infinite cylindrical cavity whose cross-section is not an ellipse has no Hill tensor. In a matrix that is isotropic in the plane of the section its response is nonetheless exact when the outside of the section is the image of the outside of a disk by a map with a finite number of terms: the complex potentials of plane elasticity are then finite sums. This page derives the concentration tensors of such a cavity, then the stress along its contour and in the matrix, and the elliptic hole in a matrix of any anisotropy of the plane, in elasticity and in conduction. The complex representation of plane elasticity and its use with a conformal map are those of Muskhelishvili, whose sections and equations are quoted where they are used; the syntax is given in Conformal holes.

1. The cavity and its three problems ​

The cavity is a cylinder of axis . Its section, in the plane , is described by the complex variable    . The matrix is isotropic, of shear modulus , Poisson ratio and Young modulus , up to section 7, which extends the result to a transversely isotropic matrix of axis ; the surface of the cavity is free. The mean strain of the cavity is defined from the displacement of its surface, of outward normal ,

and is linear in the remote stress : is the compliance contribution tensor of the cavity, per unit volume, and    its strain concentration tensor. No stress acts in the cavity, so that its stress concentration vanishes. A remote stress is the sum of three loadings, each with an exact solution:

  • a stress in the plane of the section, in plane strain (sections 3 and 4);

  • a shear , along the axis, for which the displacement is along the axis and harmonic (section 5);

  • an axial stress, which the cavity does not disturb (section 6).

A uniform axial stress is a solution in the matrix that leaves the surface of the cavity free. 7. A matrix isotropic in the plane of the section only ​

Nothing above uses the isotropy of the matrix outside the plane of the section. Let the matrix be transversely isotropic about the axis of the cavity, with Hill's moduli:    the plane-strain bulk modulus,    the shear modulus of the plane,  ,   and   the shear modulus along the axis. The three problems keep their solutions, with other constants.

In conduction the same holds: the problem of section 5 involves the conductivity of the plane only, and does not depend on it.

A material with aligned cavities whose sections have an axis of symmetry of order 3, or of order 5 and more, or are oriented at random in the plane, is such a medium. The self-consistent and the differential schemes, whose reference medium is the estimate itself, therefore apply to these cavities (Prismatic pores with corners).

8. A plate in plane stress ​

A thin plate loaded in its plane is in a state of generalized plane stress. The mean fields through its thickness satisfy the equations of plane strain with replaced by    and unchanged ((Muskhelishvili, 1977), section 26, equation (26.3)), so that becomes

(equation (32.2′)). The compliance of a hole in a plate is thus that of section 4 with the factor in place of    . In a cell of the plane the hole is given the stiffness of the plane of its matrix,     in plane strain or     in plane stress, and the factor is    or    (Plane problems). The compliance of a hole in a plate is not the plane-strain one with a zero axial stress added as in section 6: there the axial stress vanishes on average only, and the two results differ except under a hydrostatic stress of the plane.

The contour of the hole is free, and the stress is largest there: this section gives it. In the frame of the normal and the tangent to the contour, the free surface leaves   ; the only stress left is , the hoop stress, which is then the trace of the stress of the plane. Away from the contour the stress needs the second potential as well. The condition of the free contour, written between functions rational in , gives it in closed form in the whole matrix, and the powers of that cancel in it are removed on the coefficients, so that the stress keeps its digits far from the hole; the derivation is in The stress in the matrix, and matrix_stress(hole, Σ, x) gives the stress tensor at the point of the matrix, for a map of any number of terms.

10. An anisotropic matrix of the plane ​

This section says which holes are solved in a matrix of any anisotropy of the plane, and why. In such a matrix the stress derives from two holomorphic functions of the variables    ,  , where and are the roots of positive imaginary part of the characteristic equation of the compliances (The elliptic hole in an anisotropic matrix). At the point of the contour,

For the ellipse,  , the right-hand side is   : the function    maps the outside of the disk onto the outside of the image of the hole in the plane of , and takes on the circle the image of the same point of the contour as . The conditions on the contour are then written on the circle for the three functions at once, and solved in closed form. For   the powers ,  , keep the factor  , which vanishes at isotropy only (  ): continued outside the disk, the right-hand side grows as and is not the map of the outside of the image, whose map is another function. A point of the circle no longer gives the same point of the contour in the three planes.

The package therefore solves the elliptic hole, ConformalHole((m,)), in a cell of the plane whose matrix has any anisotropy: its strain concentration tensor, which is that of the ellipse given by its Hill tensor, the stress along its contour, and the stress in the matrix (The stress in the matrix). The formulas are written with the sum and the product of and , or with the mean and the divided difference of a quantity over the two roots, so that the isotropic matrix, where the two roots coincide, is an ordinary case.

In conduction the temperature is the real part of a function of the one variable    , the root of positive imaginary part of    , and the same argument holds with one plane instead of two: the insulating ellipse takes any symmetric conductivity of the plane, and its gradient concentration tensor, which is not symmetric in general, is in closed form (Conduction around the insulating ellipse); for an isotropic conductivity it is the tensor of section 5. A map of several terms in an anisotropic matrix is refused, in elasticity and in conduction.

11. Checks ​

The ellipse is the elliptic cylinder of the package, obtained from its Hill tensor: the two routes agree on every component.

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization, TensND

C₀ = iso_stiffness(1.7, 0.6)                      # bulk and shear moduli of the matrix
void = 0 * C₀
b, c = 3.0, 1.0                                   # semi-axes of the section
A_map = gradient_gradient_concentration(ConformalHole(((b - c) / (b + c),)), void, C₀)
A_hill = gradient_gradient_concentration(Cylinder(b, c), void, C₀)
maximum(abs, canonical_components(A_map) - canonical_components(A_hill))
3.197442310920451e-14

For the hypotrochoid     the system of section 3 is solved by hand. Under a hydrostatic stress in the plane,   and     alone: the area strain of the hole per unit stress, the compressibility of the pore, is

that is      times that of the circle (Ekneligoda and Zimmerman, 2006).

julia
ν, μ = (3 * 1.7 - 2 * 0.6) / (2 * (3 * 1.7 + 0.6)), 0.6
n, m = 4, 0.15
H = canonical_components(inverse_property_contribution(ConformalHole(n => m), void, C₀))
Σ = (2ν, 1.0, 1.0)                                # hydrostatic in the plane, with its axial reaction
compressibility = sum(H[i, i, j, j] * Σ[j] for i in 2:3, j in 1:3)
compressibility, 2 * (1 - ν) / μ * (1 + n * m^2) / (1 - n * m^2)
(2.6267592057065756, 2.6267592057065747)

A transversely isotropic matrix about the axis: the circular cylinder of the package, from its Hill tensor in that matrix, agrees with the map on every component.

julia
Cₜ = ti_from_constants(5.2, 1.9, 1.4, 9.0, 1.1, (1.0, 0.0, 0.0))   # C₁₁₁₁, C₁₁₂₂, C₁₁₃₃, C₃₃₃₃, C₂₃₂₃, axis third
A_map = gradient_gradient_concentration(ConformalHole(()), 0 * Cₜ, Cₜ)
A_hill = gradient_gradient_concentration(Cylinder(1.0, 1.0), 0 * Cₜ, Cₜ)
maximum(abs, canonical_components(A_map) - canonical_components(A_hill))

12. Scope ​

The solution is exact for a matrix that is isotropic, or transversely isotropic about the axis of the cavity, and for a map with a finite number of terms. A corner is reached in the limit of an infinite map only: a cut map rounds it, and the tensors converge with the number of terms (Prismatic pores with corners). The coefficients are numbers, dual numbers or symbols. ConformalHole is the inclusion, contour_stress the stress along the contour of a hole of the plane, and matrix_stress the stress at any point of its matrix, for numbers and dual numbers: the point of the circle that a point of the matrix comes from is chosen by a comparison of moduli. In a cell of the plane the ellipse is solved in a matrix of any anisotropy, in elasticity and in conduction (section 10). Outside the method are a map of several terms in a matrix anisotropic in the plane of the section, a cavity of space in such a matrix, for which the elliptic Cylinder has a Hill tensor, and holes that interact.

Where to go next ​

The complex representation used on this page is derived in the appendices Holomorphic functions and Complex potentials, and its anisotropic counterpart, for the ellipse, in The elliptic hole in an anisotropic matrix; the stress in the matrix and the insulating ellipse in an anisotropic conductor in The stress in the matrix and Conduction around the insulating ellipse. The stress along the contour and ahead of the tip is computed in an isotropic and in a plywood plate in The elliptic hole, from an isotropic to an anisotropic plate.

A shape with neither a closed form nor an exact series is the subject of the next chapter: Approximation by Gaussians presents the approximation, then Planar cracks of any contour and Heterogeneities of any shape solve with it the integral equations of a crack and of a heterogeneity.
